segments: And when the snow came,
they made an excuse of the winter, and they abandoned [the siege] and left.
Because in the Tishris of this year, which is the year 1343
(1343 of the Greeks,
1031 of our Lord,
and of the Arabs 422),
the Romans entered Edessa.
Now Nasir al-Dawlah sent an envoy to Michael and rebuked him:
"What did you gain on the two occasions when you marched out against Aleppo,
that now also you have coveted Edessa? Therefore, out of affection, I advise you to withdraw your men from it;
otherwise, you shall see what you will encounter from the force of the Arabs."
Michael, however, replied:
"I did not take Edessa by the sword,
but bought it legitimately from its owner.
And had I known that it would remain yours,
I would have restored it [to you].
However, I know
that the Ma'addite Banu Numayr will not leave it alone."
And thus, when Michael made light of the Arabs,
he sent ten thousand cavalrymen to Edessa
and rebuilt its ruins.
And the Romans began going out from Edessa
and raiding the region of Aksas, Harran, and Sarug.
And they did not cease from taking captives
until Ibn Watthab the Numayrite, the ruler of Harran, gave them tribute.
And also Hassan, the ruler of Sura, submitted to the Romans
and hung crosses upon the heads of his spears.
And in the year 423
(423 of the Arabs),
a woman in Baghdad gave birth to the likeness of a serpent of short stature,
which had the head of a human being, a mouth, and a neck,
without hands and without feet.
And when it fell further onto the ground, it spoke and said:
"Four years from now, famine will destroy mankind, unless men, women, children, and cattle go out
and kneel before the Lord so that He may send down His rain."
And when the caliph al-Qa'im heard this,
he commanded all the people to go out outside
and make supplication.
And because many did not believe this report,
only a few went out.
And in that same year, the water froze in Baghdad,
and red sand came down like rain,
and the trees were destroyed,
and they gave no fruit at all in that year.
And there was a great famine {OCR?: ܕܲܦܢܵܐ for ܟܲܦܢܵܐ} in the desert,
so that the Ma'addites there ate their camels, their horses, and even their children,
as a man would exchange his child for the child of his companion,
so that he might not feel too much grief when slaughtering him.
